records.name: South Sumatra
records.summary:
On 19 July 2026 Palembang's city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation (Perpres) No. 111 of 2025 on the national defence policy 2025-2029, which lists the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats; Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. The regulation remains in preparation, not enacted, with no specified penalty; no enforcement event is documented for this province. South Sumatra is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight's discriminatory-regulation mapping, and its neighbour Lampung saw a documented Satpol PP raid on three transwomen (November 2018) - the Sumatran belt is where local enforcement is consolidating.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT measures from moral panic to national-defence doctrine - the August 2026 ABC reporting links the 'rule that deems them a threat' to a wave of street attacks on trans women, though it cautions the trend cannot yet be confirmed - but without an enacted local penalty the traveler-facing risk here remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions.

records.name: Aguascalientes
records.summary:
Aguascalientes sits under Mexico's federal framework: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or trans presence, and legal gender recognition nationally remains a state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed legislatures to complete.

The surviving audited sources document no state-level recognition law, no hostile ordinances, and no state-specific enforcement or incident series for Aguascalientes.

records.name: Baja California
records.summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. The state congress created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure in a 2022 Civil Code reform; after the Supreme Court struck down its adults-only limit in June 2023, a new reform passed in 2024 extended recognition to children and adolescents. In May 2022 the congress also added a penal-code chapter "Crimes against Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression". The counterweight is Tijuana: the state attorney general publicly warned of a serial killer of women in prostitution there (at least 3 victims; suspect arrested July 2023 after an Interpol notice and FBI cooperation), only 22 of 278 killed women in the state were classed as feminicides, and a 2021 burning of a trans woman's body in her Tijuana home is recorded within that pattern. Mixed: protective law, under-counted lethal risk concentrated in one border city.

records.name: Baja California Sur
records.summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. The state congress created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure by Civil Code reform in 2021; after the Supreme Court ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents was unconstitutional, a 2024 reform expanded the right. Baja California Sur also recognises the transfemicide offence. No region-specific incident or enforcement pattern was found; visitor-facing risk tracks the national baseline.

records.name: Campeche
records.summary:
Campeche is among the Mexican states that have embraced the reform direction: its congress passed a 2024 Civil Code reform creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, following the national supreme court's rulings pressing states to provide one. Identity documents can therefore be aligned locally without litigation — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in a country where mismatched documents drive questioning and denials.

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinances or enforcement incidents against trans people appear in the audited sources. National context remains violent for trans people, and other states' transfemicide laws (Mexico City's 2024 statute being the benchmark) frame reform elsewhere; Campeche's own record in the surviving sources is defined by its recognition procedure rather than by documented incidents.

records.name: Chiapas
records.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal and no law targets trans presence, but Chiapas is one of ten of Mexico's 32 states whose legislatures had still created no legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, despite supreme-court doctrine establishing the right. The practical consequence is permanently mismatched identity documents for trans people — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico, since document mismatch triggers questioning at checkpoints, banks and clinics — with no local administrative cure; courts can order recognition case by case.

Rights reporting on a neighbouring non-reforming state (an unsolved killing of a trans activist, health staff outting patients, no hate-motivation provisions) illustrates the institutional climate such refusal sustains, though no Chiapas-specific violence series is documented in the surviving sources. Mexico City's 2024 transfemicide law marks the reform benchmark this state has not followed.

records.name: Chihuahua
records.summary:
Chihuahua has functioning gender-recognition machinery without a state statute: after the state civil code still required a judicial process, a 2019 supreme-court ruling struck that requirement down, and the civil registry now performs administrative recognitions. The state legislature itself had enacted no recognition law as of March 2025. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinance is documented in the surviving sources.

The surviving audited sources for this record document no state-specific incident series; the national backdrop for trans people remains violent and impunity-prone, with the capital's 2024 transfemicide law the reform benchmark other states are measured against.

records.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
records.summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. In 2018 the state congress passed a Civil Registry law establishing an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity - among the earlier such enactments in Mexico - and no region-specific incident or enforcement pattern was found; visitor-facing risk tracks the national baseline.
